description: Calm Signal is a small team from Hsinchu, Taiwan, with backgrounds in medical-imaging AI, scheduling optimization, and running AI locally so sensitive data never has to leave the premises. Team members have worked on award-winning medical AI research and passed four tracks at the 2026 Taiwan Connectathon. We are building an offline crew health review dashboard with a local AI summary. Welcome: software, data, and human-factors skills.
summary:
Near Mars, a message to Earth can take up to 22 minutes, so crew medical decisions can't wait for the ground. Calm Signal is an offline crew health self-review that runs on the spacecraft: an on-device AI drafts plain-language summaries next to explainable rule-based flags, so health data never leaves the vehicle. AI suggests; the crew decides.

It combines simulated vitals, sleep and mood with real NASA OSDR RadLab ISS radiation data, and a built-in self-test checks every number the AI writes. Six scenarios are tied to NASA Human Research Program risks.

On return, it builds an HL7 FHIR R4 handoff for sea, air and ground medical teams (simulated). Team members received a 2026 SMART on FHIR national Top 50 award in Taiwan and joined the 2026 Taiwan Connectathon.
details:
Calm Signal is a crew health self-review that keeps working when Earth is minutes away. It is a self-contained web page (HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no external libraries) that runs offline in a browser, with no account and no server required. Health data stays on the device.

What it does

- Shows a 14-day session of vitals, sleep and mood (SIMULATED, labeled on every view) next to real public ISS radiation data from NASA OSDR RadLab (DosTel1 absorbed dose rate, 19 Mar–1 Apr 2022).

- Flags days that need a closer look using simple, transparent rules (e.g. sleep at or below 5.0 h, mood at or below 2, heart rate 15 bpm above the early-day mean). The rule text is shown with every flag. Rules are illustrative, not NASA thresholds or clinical criteria.

- On-device AI: a summary request is sent only to a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint the crew sets. Without a local model, the page shows a clearly labeled recorded output from an on-device model for the same request. A built-in self-test checks that every radiation number in the AI text matches the RadLab source. AI suggests; the crew decides.

- Six field-checked scenarios (sleep, isolation, cardiovascular, radiation, comms delay, splashdown), each linked to a NASA Human Research Program risk page.

- Earth-link blackout mode: the review keeps working with no connection.

- Recovery handoff: on return, it builds an HL7 FHIR R4 bundle (LOINC codes, UCUM units) for sea, air and ground medical teams. Simulated here; nothing is sent.

Why it matters

Deep-space crews cannot wait 20+ minutes for ground advice, and medical data should not have to leave the vehicle. The same on-premise, privacy-first design fits remote clinics, ships and disaster sites on Earth.

Team: members received a 2026 SMART on FHIR national Top 50 award (Taiwan) and took part in the 2026 Taiwan Connectathon. Decision support only, not a medical device, not clinically validated. SI use is described in the SI field.
